status: Three residual source duties accounted for through supplied source-bound original scenarios and unchanged contributors. This is authoring/task design, not real-building assessment, observed pupil success or disaster-outcome certification.

wind.locator: High Winds Safety Rules and HIGH WINDS main sections
wind.readScope: Complete selected main safety/effects/preparation text read, no image inspection.
wind.facts: Strong winds break branches, topple trees, loosen objects and damage buildings, with disruption to transport/power. This supports structural and social effects, not a measured local loss prediction.

urban.locator: High Winds main causes/effects and What to Do Before sections
urban.readScope: Main body read; no warning-speed inventory, current channel reliability or image inspection claimed.
urban.facts: City guidance includes securing construction/building equipment and loose objects before an event; trees and debris can damage structures and disrupt services.

roof.locator: Scope and Description opening strengthening roof/deck/wall connections
roof.readScope: Scope/Description main mechanism paragraphs read; not all long technical tabs, compliance rules, figures or linked guides.
roof.facts: Strengthened roof-wall/deck connections resist uplift and bracing can resist earthquake shear. Opening protection addresses debris damage; these do not guarantee every structure survives.

alaska.locator: Alaska Sea Grant/UAF, June 2020; printed 12–14/PDF 11–13 windstorms; printed 26–28/PDF 25–27 foundation/connections
alaska.readScope: Actual selected main text and introductory attribution/disclaimer read; diagrams not visually read and no whole 34-page review asserted.
alaska.facts: The handbook discusses wind exposure, roof/window protection and ties connecting roof to foundation; post/pad buildings need supported stable foundations and suitable connections. It advises professional assessment because conditions and building types differ. No universal DIY specification is adopted.

quake.locator: Ground Shaking and Surface Faulting sections, source attributed to Hays 1981
quake.readScope: Complete selected ground-shaking/surface-faulting body read; no seismic-wave speed/height/frequency claims taught or figure inspection.
quake.facts: Ground shaking can vibrate/damage buildings; site and construction affect consequences. Underground fault movement and structural surface effects are distinguished.

slope.locator: Complete opening FAQ answer before Related resources
slope.readScope: Actual full FAQ answer read, not linked studies or videos.
slope.facts: Gravity drives downslope soil/rock movement; earthquake shaking can trigger failure where loading exceeds material resistance. Local strength, water and other factors matter.

wind-tree.setting: Original illustrative wooded community edge, not a measured disaster record.
wind-tree.forceAndEffect: Wind pushes/bends branches and trunk; severe loading can break limbs or topple a tree. Relate that loading and anchorage to the structural effect, not merely identify windy weather.
wind-tree.society: A falling branch/tree can obstruct access or damage power infrastructure, disrupting travel/services as reported in the weather guidance.
wind-tree.environment: Damage removes or alters living tree structure and associated habitat. A fictional before/after habitat sketch may illustrate the consequence; no counted ecological loss/recovery is claimed.
wind-tree.method: Compare assessed tree management and securing nearby objects with structural roof improvements; one method does not address every force or habitat effect.
wind-tree.limit: Tree condition, soil/root support and wind vary; do not infer a failure speed or prescribe pupil tree work.

wind-roof.setting: Original illustrative occupied timber-frame house, with stated loose roof-wall connection.
wind-roof.forceAndEffect: Supplied wind-uplift/loading account can pull weak roof connections apart; flying debris can strike openings. Stronger suitable connections and impact protection act on different failure routes.
wind-roof.society: Damage can displace occupants and interrupt services; repairs and suitable professional access have costs. No invented price or guaranteed savings is supplied.
wind-roof.environment: Damaged structures/materials can become debris; compare keeping sound material in service with replacement material/waste, as an explicitly reasoned consequence rather than measured lifecycle totals.
wind-roof.method: Professional roof-wall connection strengthening and suitable opening protection, distinguishing resistance to uplift from resistance to debris impact.
wind-roof.limit: Source examples concern particular existing homes, not all roofs or a Canadian building-code certificate.

quake-slope.setting: Original illustrative steep rock/soil slope with a nearby route; no real slope safety assessment.
quake-slope.forceAndEffect: Earthquake shaking can disturb a marginally stable slope, after which gravity moves material downhill when resistance is exceeded. Distinguish trigger, gravitational loading and the resulting fall/slide.
quake-slope.society: A supplied fictional route below the slope can be obstructed; explain why siting and professional hazard assessment matter without inventing a real road closure.
quake-slope.environment: Rock/soil movement changes landform and can cover vegetation; extent and recovery require evidence not provided here.
quake-slope.method: Use a qualified hazard/siting assessment rather than assume a roof strap stabilises a whole cliff.
quake-slope.limit: Not all earthquakes trigger all slopes and not all landslides are earthquakes; water, material and geometry influence risk.

quake-building.setting: Original illustrative house whose foundation/frame connections are described as weak.
quake-building.forceAndEffect: Ground motion makes supports move and the frame deform; inadequate connections can separate. A supported tied load path/bracing helps resist the stated movement, without making the shaking disappear.
quake-building.society: Occupant access to shelter/services can be affected; assess repair/reinforcement and disruption rather than assuming stronger always means affordable.
quake-building.environment: Damage creates material debris and rebuilding demands; no life-cycle comparison is inferred without actual data.
quake-building.method: Suitable professionally designed frame/foundation connections/bracing, supplied by the technical sources. Compare to wind-opening protection to show hazard-method fit.
quake-building.limit: No promise that any tie pattern makes any building safe, no calculated seismic capacity or instruction to carry out retrofit work.

urban-method.setting: Original fictional dense town block: roofs/building equipment above pedestrians, adjacent properties, limited work space; an inspection service and trained contractor can be scheduled. These are supplied case facts, not universal traits of cities.
urban-method.structure: Built roof/equipment/openings on a specified building.
urban-method.forceAndEffect: Wind can lift loose components and throw debris towards nearby structures/people.
urban-method.method: Secure loose construction/equipment before the event and have qualified adults assess roof connections/opening protection, using the supplied sources.
urban-method.suitability: Nearby exposure makes preventing falling/flying components relevant; plan work access and affected neighbours as well as the physical connection.
urban-method.constraint: A building owner/qualified contractor must choose suitable work; a pupil cannot certify another property or transfer one low-rise detail to every tall building.

rural-method.setting: Original fictional rural timber-frame home: an exposed plot, accessible roof space, road access for a qualified contractor, limited repair budget and a nearby mature tree. Facts are supplied for the task, not inferred from a rural label.
rural-method.structure: Roof/wall and nearby tree as separate structures.
rural-method.forceAndEffect: Wind uplift can separate a weak roof connection; branch fall is a distinct loading/impact route.
rural-method.method: Compare professionally assessed roof-wall ties with appropriate tree inspection/management and opening protection. Explain what each would and would not address.
rural-method.suitability: The specified accessible structure permits assessment of a roof retrofit; compare budget/need rather than prescribe replacement of sound materials. Tree work and roof work solve different routes to harm.
rural-method.constraint: Accessibility and affordability are given rather than assumed for all rural places; pupils recommend a reasoned priority and identify further information, not a construction specification.

remote-method.setting: Original fictional remote community building: pad/post foundation, exposed coastal winds, seasonal delivery of replacement parts and a limited visiting-contractor window. Local knowledge and qualified inspection inform the case; no real community is labelled unsafe.
remote-method.forceAndEffect: Wind loading and possible ground/support movement can affect different connections; a tied roof alone cannot repair an unstable foundation.
remote-method.method: Assess foundation stability and suitable continuous connections with qualified advice, plan inspection/parts in the stated delivery window, and compare with securing loose items/opening protection before storms.
remote-method.suitability: The whole support path and the explicit access/maintenance schedule matter. A method needing unavailable materials or unverified ground anchorage is conditional rather than automatically suitable.
remote-method.constraint: Alaska 2020 supplies introductory mechanism/examples, not a universal law for remote/Indigenous communities, permafrost or Ontario codes. No rapid on-demand specialist service is assumed.

sourceAndScopeLimits: Scenario constraints are original explicitly supplied fictional facts; verified sources support mechanisms, not a claim that these places were surveyed or that real retrofits succeeded.

Actual source duties require analysis/methods across community settings; no particular real locality or child-owned building is mandatory. These fully prepared scenarios avoid an unfilled own-place resource dependency.

All existing full cards/guides/hard paths remain intact; no older quantitative bundle, pressure equation, base-isolation requirement for every source case or country-specific building code is imported.

Natural structural effects and human-built damage, society/environment consequences and all three setting-specific method justifications must actually be assessed, not inferred from association counts.
consumerBoundary: Four overall component associations only, no claim/guide/age/dependency changes or learner-state action.
